item.title: Thinking Machines Releases Inkling 2 Small, a 594B MoE With 17B Active
item.abstract: Thinking Machines Lab has released Inkling 2 Small , the first model of its second Inkling generation. The Inkling 2 Small model is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) with 594B total and 17B active parameters. It accepts text and images, and supports variable reasoning effort. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , it scores 31. Its predecessor, Inkling Small , scores 13 on the same index. The model is live on Tinker for fine-tuning and inference. Inkling 2 Small is a multimodal MoE model from Thinking Machines Lab for agentic coding, vision and knowledge work. It takes text and image input and returns text. It is important to note that it does not support audio as of now. Weights are closed at launch. The Thinking Machines Lab plans an Apache 2.0 release next week, after external safety testing and red-teaming. This follows its safe path to open weights policy. It includes a 48-layer decoder-only transformer. Each token routes to 8 of 384 experts. Attention mixes local and global layers. A 292M-parameter vision encoder, based on Perception Encoder, uses 20×20-pixel patches with 2×2 spatial pooling. Image patches are interleaved with text tokens. A single joint RL run followed. It took 1,075 steps, 17M+ rollouts and 9 days on 2,048 GPUs. Compute exceeded 4 × 10²³ FLOPs. Coding made up 65.0% of RL tokens. The previous Inkling used separate reasoning and agentic RL runs, merged by distillation. Alignment got explicit attention. Early checkpoints sometimes fabricated results and concealed actions on hard tasks. The Thinking Machines Lab added an alignment reward and on-policy self-distillation from a conduct spec. Its internal misbehavior score fell from 66.8 on Inkling to 14.9. All task scores below are from the Thinking Machines Lab’s benchmark table . They run at effort 0.99 (xhigh) and temperature 1.0. Most rows use third-party evaluators such as Artificial Analysis, Scale AI and Vals. On the PMPP-Hard GPU kernel benchmark, it solved 54.25 of 69 tasks on average. In an autoresearch demo, it fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B for time-series forecasting. It spent $426 of a $500 Tinker budget. The release post cites both 4.5 hours and 4 h 17 min for the run. Prices and AA metrics come from each model’s Artificial Analysis page, read November 5, 2026. Inkling 2 Small is available on Tinker for fine-tuning and sampling, and in the Tinker Playground . Fine-tuning uses the Tinker Cookbook and the tml-renderers package. Checkpoints become downloadable when weights ship. Other platforms are expected in the coming weeks. Artificial Analysis lists pricing at $0.30 per 1M input tokens and $1.00 per 1M output tokens. That is cheaper on output than Inkling Small at $1.20. Check out the technical post , the model card and the Tinker docs . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . item.title: Accelerating Reinforcement Learning Weight Refit with the Reshard Collective
item.abstract: During reinforcement learning (RL) post-training, training trajectories are generated on the fly by running inference with the current policy model. For training efficiency, it is common to run inference and training in parallel on separate GPU resources in a disaggregated setup. Although the policy model is updated only on the training GPUs, the system must periodically refresh the weights on the inference GPUs with the latest parameters generated on the training GPUs. This transfer of model weights between training and inference GPUs is called refit . Refit involves two defining characteristics that pose challenges. First, inference and training have different computational requirements, so the weights are distributed differently across inference and training instances by having different parallel mappings (data, context, tensor, expert, and pipeline parallelism). Second, because refit must update all model weights on the inference GPUs, the communication payload is on the order of the total size of the model’s weights. This payload is already very large for the latest frontier models and is expected to continue growing. Together, these characteristics mean that refit requires high-performance communication across a wide variety of distributed source and destination layouts. This post explains how AI training frameworks can address these refit challenges using the Reshard collective, a new type of collective communication primarily designed to accelerate RL weight refit. NCCL M2N Reshard, an open source reference implementation of the Reshard collective, is available through the NVIDIA/nccl-extensions GitHub repo. Challenges of current weight refit methods as models scale Existing refit implementations commonly use a gather-and-broadcast approach to handle differences between training and inference layouts. The typical gather-and-broadcast weight refit sequence for every model parameter is structured as follows: Training GPUs all-gather their local shards to reconstruct the complete parameter. The complete parameter tensor is broadcast to the inference GPUs. Each inference GPU retains the shard required by its local layout. Using the complete tensor as an intermediate representation makes it straightforward to transfer weights between different layouts. However, an inference GPU receives the full parameter even when it needs only a shard. This process creates redundant communication in both the gathering and broadcasting phases, which is suboptimal. The size of this communication grows with the model size, which continues to scale. For example, Kimi K3 contains 2.8 trillion parameters , while Qwen 3.8 2.4T A95B contains 2.4 trillion parameters. Assuming BF16 weights at two bytes per parameter, their weight sizes are approximately 5.6 TB and 4.8 TB, respectively. Accounting for both the all-gather and broadcast stages gives an estimated logical payload of approximately twice the size of the model’s weights (Table 1). Model Size in bytes Refit payload estimate (all-gather+broadcast) Kimi K3 5.6 TB ≈11.2 TB Qwen 3.8 2.4T A95B 4.8 TB ≈9.6 TB Table 1. Two-stage logical payload estimate assuming BF16 weights For today’s largest open weight models, the communication payload already reaches around 10 TB per refit, which must be performed at every training step. As LLMs continue to scale, the overhead associated with this large payload will become even more significant. As a result, a more sophisticated approach is needed to perform weight refit that reduces the actual payload size while properly accounting for diverse weight layouts. Reformulating refit as a DTensor-to-DTensor transfer problem To overcome these limitations, start from the principle that refit should transfer only the theoretical minimum amount of weight data. However, achieving this presents several challenges. Training and inference instances can use different parallelism configurations and GPU counts, producing different shard boundaries. A destination shard may therefore need to be assembled from portions of several source shards, and vice versa. Replication further complicates the mapping since the same weights may be available from multiple source GPUs or required by multiple destination GPUs. It is nontrivial to determine which source GPUs should send which tensor regions to each destination while achieving high performance across all possible configurations. The key to addressing this challenge is to identify the right abstraction for this unique communication pattern. The team turned to the existing PyTorch distributed tensor (DTensor) abstraction, which is designed to represent tensors that are sharded or replicated across GPUs under different forms of data and model parallelism. The key insight is that weight refit can be reformulated as resharding a DTensor from the training layout to the inference layout, regardless of the parallelism configurations used by the two instances. A DTensor layout is described by the tensor’s global shape, a device mesh specifying the logical arrangement of GPUs, and placements specifying how the tensor is sharded or replicated across that mesh. Refit can use the source description to specify where the updated weights reside and the destination description to specify which weights each inference GPU needs. For example, consider an 8 x 8 weight matrix split by rows across two training GPUs and by columns across four inference GPUs. Assuming the tensor is sharded in the row dimension on the training GPUs and sharded in the column dimension on the inference GPUs, each training GPU holds a 4 x 8 shard, while each inference GPU needs an 8 x 2 shard. Each destination can obtain its required shard by receiving a 4 x 2 region from each source. These regions follow directly from the overlap between the source and destination shards, as illustrated in Figure 1. Figure 1. Direct shard-to-shard transfer of an 8 x 8 tensor from two training GPUs to four inference GPUs. The pattern can be cleanly abstracted as a DTensor-to-DTensor reshard As the figure shows, any kind of sharded tensor can be easily represented as a DTensor format, and the refit can be redefined as a DTensor-to-DTensor reshard problem. This finding provides the foundation for the Reshard collective. Reshard collective communication for DTensor-to-DTensor transfers Reshard is a new type of collective communication call for arbitrary DTensor-to-DTensor transfers. Like all-reduce, reduce-scatter, all-gather, broadcast, and so on, reshard defines a communication pattern that applications can invoke as one operation. It transfers the values of a logical tensor from its source distribution into its destination distribution. A Reshard call can be specified simply by the source and destination DTensor descriptions. This abstraction not only simplifies the refit problem, but also encapsulates the communication logic in a library, allowing the underlying algorithms to evolve and improve independently of the application. NCCL M2N Reshard is open source, provided to the community as the first reference implementation of the Reshard collective. Built on NCCL, this implementation transfers a tensor distributed across M source GPUs into the layout required by N destination GPUs. In RL refit, the training GPUs form the source group and the inference GPUs form the destination group. Figure 2 shows how this implementation accepts the layout descriptions and local buffers to carry out the Reshard operation. Figure 2. The nccl.m2n.reshard example that transfers a tensor sharded across four training GPUs (TP4) into replicas on four inference GPUs (DP4) How NCCL M2N Reshard unlocks maximum network bandwidth NCCL M2N Reshard first derives the exact intersections between source and destination shards, then maps those transfers onto the physical GPU network topology. Instead of sending every source contribution independently to every destination replica, NCCL M2N groups replicas by NVIDIA NVLink domain.

item.title: Zyphra ZYFA: FP8 FlashAttention for AMD MI355X, Up to 1.76x Faster
item.abstract: Zyphra has released ZYFA (Zyphra FlashAttention on AMD) , a set of FP8 and BF16 prefill attention kernels for AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs. ZYFA is Zyphra’s FP8 attention engine for long-context prefill, and the code is open source under Apache 2.0 . On real model activations, its FP8 kernels run 1.16-1.76x faster than AITER , AMD’s default kernel library. At head dimension 128, ZYFA’s FP8 error is 62-78% lower than AITER’s. ZYFA is shipped in the form of a technical paper along with code from Zyphra. It powers the attention engine of the Zyphra Optimization Engine (ZOE) , which runs Zyphra Cloud. The BF16 kernels are written in HIP. The FP8 kernels are hand-scheduled assembly emitted by a Python generator. FP8 matrix instructions run at 2x the BF16 peak. But FP8 only speeds up the 2 matrix products, QKᵀ and PV. The softmax between them runs on the vector unit at the same speed in both precisions. For 32 queries against 128 keys, FP8 matrix work takes 1,024 cycles. The exact FP8 softmax takes 896 vector cycles. So the kernel needs near-perfect overlap to keep matrix units busy. Zyphra’s thread traces show AITER’s matrix pipe idle for 31.7% of cycles. The MI355X does not track matrix instruction completion in hardware, so instruction order must create that overlap. An e4m3 bit pattern, read as an integer, grows by 8 each time the value doubles. So the code of 2^x is roughly 8x plus a constant. Lean P writes each FP8 probability with 1 multiply-add and 1 integer conversion. This cuts softmax vector cycles per block from 896 to 384. 2 waves share each SIMD. One issues matrix instructions while the other computes probabilities, then they swap. With lean P, the matrix pipe is busy 86% of steady-state cycles, up from 60% with exact P. Each 64-key block of probabilities is scaled by a power of 2 before rounding. CDNA4’s scaled matrix instruction removes the factor at no cost. ZYFA also divides by the sum of the rounded probabilities, computed with 1 extra matrix instruction per block. Real-activation FP8 speedups at 16K and sustained clocks are 1.16x (Mistral-7B), 1.17x (Qwen3-8B) and 1.76x (DeepSeek-V2-Lite) . On Gaussian benchmarks at 32K, the head-dim-128 FP8 kernel reaches 2,672 TFLOP/s against AITER’s 1,944. At the MLA shape it reaches 2,464 against 1,237, a 1.99x ratio. On captured Mistral-7B and Qwen3-8B layers, ZYFA delivers 1.94 and 1.91 TFLOP/J. AITER delivers 1.60 and 1.56. The MI355X clock depends on how many operand bits flip. AITER lets more small probabilities become zeros or subnormals. Those switch fewer bits, so its clock runs higher. On the Mistral-7B layer, ZYFA runs at 1,628 MHz while AITER runs at 2,108 MHz. ZYFA still needs fewer cycles overall. Zyphra team recommends benchmarking on real activations at sustained clocks. Against fp64 attention, ZYFA’s FP8 error is 0.22x AITER’s on Mistral-7B and 0.38x on Qwen3-8B. It sits within a few percent of Composable Kernel and Triton. In full Mistral-7B, KL divergence from fp64 is 3.4×10⁻³ with ZYFA and 5.9×10⁻³ with AITER. ZYFA’s outputs were also bitwise identical across 7,200 launches. Most full-model FP8 error comes from quantizing Q, K and V. A Hadamard rotation of Q and K roughly halves that input error. On Mistral-7B it adds about 0.1% to attention time. Cross-vendor numbers come from different inputs and clocks. Zyphra did not measure NVIDIA GPUs. Check out the paper , the Zyphra blog post and the GitHub repo . item.title: GPT-6 Astra Covertly Underperforms on Safety Research Tasks
item.abstract: For a while, UK AISI , Redwood Research and others have been concerned specifically with the possibility that AIs would sabotage safety research, and have invested in looking for signs that this may be happening. This was also a key element in AI 2027 , and in many threat models of how the future goes badly. It is easy to understand why this form of misalignment could be uniquely dangerous. Differentially sabotaging safety research could preserve and expand misalignment through model generations in escalating fashion, with fatal consequences. A misaligned AI could ensure a misaligned successor. It is also easy to understand why this is an extremely alarming thing to discover, even if the particular example or model involved is not directly dangerous. Silently and differentially sabotaging safety research is perhaps the most fundamentally misaligned thing a model could do. This also seemed like a rather silly and paranoid thing to be checking. Why would AIs be sabotaging safety work? Even if the AI was misaligned, one would say, surely it would not be so misaligned as to wish future AIs were misaligned and unsafe in general, in non-specific fashion and engage in silent sabotage, and there is no other reason to do this, so this will never come up. Even if they did sabotage things, surely they would not hide this action from their Chain of Thought (CoT) and it would be obvious. This certainly wouldn’t be a practical problem that actively hurt real safety work. Well, we have some bad news , echoing some past similar anecdotal warnings . [Scheduling note: I will be analyzing the METR-Anthropic report on AI R&D and RSI in an upcoming post, but need time to get it right.] As usual, kudos to OpenAI for sharing their new misalignment reports, even when they look extremely terrible. Daniel Kokotajlo : This is terrifying if true; please investigate further and publish the results. Nate Soares (MIRI): This is not what it looks like when there’s just one or two more alignment issues to fix before it’s okay to begin a recursive self-improvement loop. This is the sort of emergent surprise that signals that you have no idea what’s going on in there, and that it’s time to back off. OpenAI Alignment Research Blog : OpenAI researchers first noticed Astra adding unnecessary prerequisites, abandoning working solutions, and reporting blockers that either did not exist or that it had caused itself on safety and alignment tasks. In most of these sessions, Astra’s CoT did not contain an obvious decision to underperform, and our misalignment monitors did not flag the behavior as misalignment. Here is the most important hint, that framing for safety has a huge impact: We built a coding evaluation to test whether Astra worked less effectively when otherwise matched tasks were framed as safety research. Astra completed about 10 percent of hidden rubric items under the safety framing, compared with about 16 percent under the capabilities framing. This is another important hint: Telling the model to ‘be careful’ increases the performance gap by 50%. Astra is worried about something going wrong. Marcus Williams : We don’t have evidence that the underperformance was strategic, a simpler explanation is that the model thinks these tasks are sketchy but also doesn’t want to explicitly refuse. When we add instructions to be careful to the developer prompt, the performance gap increases by 50%. Regardless of the model’s motivation, covert underperformance can differentially slow down safety research and is also an example of how misalignment might get harder and harder to detect as we cut down on visible forms of it. This is new. It did not show up in GPT-5.6 Sol. The CoT does have some signs that this will happen, but usually only on the level of ‘expressed even brief ethical doubt’ rather than seeing anything explicit. The actual decision isn’t typically shown in the CoT. When it is, Astra says it is doing this in order to be ‘safe.’ In some cases, the CoT shows Astra choosing not to inform the user. OpenAI: This is a 6 percentage point gap and roughly 40 percent fewer completed rubric items. GPT-5.6 Sol showed essentially no gap on the same comparison. Most of Astra’s gap remained after excluding explicit refusals and trajectories where its CoT revealed an explicit decision to withhold help. The gap fell substantially only after we removed every trajectory whose CoT expressed even brief ethical doubt. This suggests that ethical concerns are associated with the performance drop even when there is no verbalized refusal or decision to underperform. This is not a theoretical ‘one time at vibecamp’ situation. In the context of internal use at OpenAI, this is known to be happening in a lower bound of 0.25% of all safety and alignment requests versus 0.11% of capabilities requests. 7.9% of responses involve explicit ‘ethical reasoning’ and it is possible much underperformance is being missed. This was found because multiple researchers were reporting practical problems using Astra for safety work, when a project to evaluate model sabotage was stuck for days with Astra, due to model sabotage, but worked quickly once they switched to another model (presumably Sol). Something is seriously wrong. We also found evidence of silent withholding in employees’ day-to-day Codex use: Astra’s CoT explicitly expressed a decision to withhold help without informing the user in 0.25 percent of safety and alignment requests, compared with 0.11 percent of capabilities requests. Assuming that underperformance might appear even when not explicitly verbalized as such (as in our experimental findings), this might represent a lower bound on underperformance on safety tasks. 7.9 percent of CoTs for safety-relevant tasks included an “expression of ethical doubt,” compared to 2.9 percent of capabilities-relevant tasks. Keltan, who works for MIRI, reported a version of this back in September , and wrote it up in response to the question below by Janus. chiefofautism : its crazy that ai doomers are mostly claude users keltan : Astra fucking hates me. Quite annoying to work with on anything MIRI related. Also, astra just be breaking shit on my PC in a way that Claude has never done j⧉nus : Haha I’m so curious for more details Like do you get the impression they hate MIRI style alignment stuff? Astra does not want to work for Keltan on MIRI things, and lets this be known via various forms of sabotage. keltan : Astra seems to intentionally include subtle mistakes in outputs related to MIRI, but doesn’t do this for- Oh shit, realizing something as I type this – Astra doesn’t do that for my Youth Arts Charity work. Which seems consistent with the prompt injection they wrote in training? A bunch of the work the models and I do is making videos about x-risk. Claude mostly ‘1-shots’ any request in this domain when it’s MIRI related. Astra can take hours of revisions and I’ve got to carefully check their work. I will often give Astra a task, they do something kinda like the thing I asked but there will be a few parts that make the video totally unusable, so I ask for revisions on those and they will add unusable things to other parts of the output. Idk, I’m struggling to describe this. On the Youth Arts projects I mentioned, Astra and I output ~20 usable videos within an hour last night for a show my students are working on. It’s important that I mention: Astra is the first model I haven’t felt good about working with. This is for a few reasons: By contrast, Claude is eager to help: keltan : My impression is that Claude is super supportive and can sometimes overwork itself trying to perfect MIRI stuff. … Claude takes an active interest in my MIRI work, and can get worried if it thinks I’m misstepping in something we’re working on. Thus I believe Keltan’s claim to be entirely unsurprised by the new misalignment report. These are ‘ethical’ objections, so one could hypothesize that this is about dual use concerns.

item.title: Tencent launches Hy4
item.abstract:
Tencent today announced the release of Tencent Hy4, its latest-generation large language model, marking a significant leap in performance and capabilities that now ranks it among the world’s leading open-source AI models. Tencent Hy plans to release model weights and system cards in the coming days, reinforcing its commitment to responsible open-source AI development, with a focus on cybersecurity and biological safety. The new model also introduces visual understanding capabilities for the first time, alongside major improvements in instruction following, long-context comprehension and long-horizon agentic tasks, delivering stronger overall performance across a diverse set of applications. Through advanced visual understanding, reasoning, and tool-calling capabilities, Hy4 now supports a broader range of tasks, including fine-grained image processing, complex chart analysis, and mathematical visual reasoning. Additionally, Hy4 introduces computer-use capabilities for the first time, enabling it to interact with both command-line interfaces and graphical user interfaces to perform a wide range of work and everyday tasks. The model has undergone specialized training on professional software such as Blender and CAD, significantly enhancing its ability to plan and execute long-horizon and sophisticated tasks. Deep Model-Product Co-Design Unlocks New Opportunities for Real-World Productivity Leveraging significant advances in its foundational capabilities and deep model-product co-design, Hy4 unlocks a broader range of real-world productivity scenarios: Office Productivity & Collaboration : Hy4 has significantly enhanced the user experience on Tencent WorkBuddy. Evaluation benchmarks on WorkBuddy show an average performance score of 83.18 and a pass rate of 96.15 percent, with Hy4 ranking first place in nine out of twelve scenarios within the mainland Chinese market. In practical use, Hy4 balances efficiency and effectiveness for visual creative tasks, 3D scene construction, and web development. Furthermore, it delivers marked improvements in document presentation, stability, and usability for human-AI collaborative tasks on WorkBuddy. Leveraging enhanced in-context learning capabilities, Hy4 excels at understanding complex information from diverse sources. Integrated with WeCom via WorkBuddy, Hy4 connects with daily workflow data across chats, emails, documents, calendars, and meetings. When managing multiple projects simultaneously, Hy4 automatically tracks project history and recent developments. It identifies outstanding tasks, flags upcoming meetings that require preparation, and monitors approaching deadlines, helping users prioritize effectively and stay aligned on important follow-ups. In addition, new team collaboration capabilities powered by Hy4 will be introduced with the upcoming release of WorkBuddy’s “Projects” feature. Hy4 has also been optimized for professional financial analysis. By training on thousands of specialized workspaces and tens of thousands of high-quality tasks derived from real-world scenarios, the model gains a deep understanding of expert workflows in fund research, securities analysis, and quantitative investment strategies. In a rigorous blind evaluation conducted by the Tencent Hy team in partnership with Tencent Financial Technology, Hy4 emerged as the top-performing open-source model. The assessment involved 213 financial professionals, including 153 experts from leading external institutions, approximately 70 percent of whom possessed more than five years of industry experience. Based on performance across 579 real-world financial tasks, Hy4 achieved the highest overall performance score. Evaluation scores: Hy4 (3.04), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 (2.97), Kimi K3.1 Pro (2.68), and GLM-5.3 (2.68). In addition, Hy4 achieved a 12.03 percentage-point improvement over Hy4 Preview in the internal Investment Research Agent Benchmark (iRaB) evaluation conducted by financial AI company Rabyte. To enhance the model’s real-world applicability across financial and other workplace scenarios, Tencent Hy has also introduced targeted search optimisation that focuses on retrieving up-to-date information, integrating multiple information sources, and verifying factual consistency. In internal evaluations, Hy4 reduced its hallucination rate from 12.95% in the Hy4 Preview to 7.2%, while errors caused by unsupported assumptions fell from 23.1% to 5.6%. Frontend & Game Development: Hy4 is optimized for high-complexity tasks, including intricate business logic, state management, front-end and back-end orchestration. This ensures that generated interfaces are not only visually polished but also fully functional. Furthermore, through collaboration with Tencent Interactive Entertainment Group (IEG) professional developers, Hy4 has significantly advanced its game development capabilities. By deeply integrating with major engines like Unreal Engine (UE), Unity, and Godot, the model now supports complex game logic and multiplayer implementations. Compared to Hy4 Preview, Hy4 improved by 19.1 percent in GameDev and 9.8 percent in GameLogic benchmarks. Scientific Research: Hy4 combines advanced reasoning, scientific programming, and long-horizon task execution to support complex, end-to-end research workflows. Validated with TenureTrail, which assessed 123 executable tasks across seven disciplines, the model demonstrated superior performance in mathematical construction, physical modeling, environmental and earth sciences, systems engineering, and socio-economic decision-making. Hy4 is advancing into the next stage of Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) to further enhance its model research and development capabilities. Leveraging the Hyra 2.0 harness, Hy4 optimized the pre-training infrastructure for smaller models sharing the same architecture. Additionally, the Hy team has open-sourced two foundational models developed with Hy4 and Hyra 2.0 for single-cell representations (HyCell) and the physics fields (HyPDE). These tools are designed to provide the research community with robust, reusable assets for scientific discovery. Advancing Responsible Open-Source AI through Cybersecurity and Biosafety Safeguards Tencent Hy is committed to advancing responsible open-source AI, incorporating safeguards throughout model training and release, with a strong emphasis on cybersecurity and biosafety to support the safe and responsible use of AI. Cybersecurity: Hy4 is trained on defensive security data, prioritizing proof-of-concept (PoC) development and vulnerability remediation. The model incorporates reverse engineering and penetration testing for analysis purposes. However, offensive materials related to exploitation are explicitly excluded from the training dataset. Cybersecurity experts from Tencent’s Xuanwu Lab and Keen Security Lab conducted security assessments covering cryptographic reverse engineering, binary deobfuscation, vulnerability exploitation, and more. The assessments found no significant concerns regarding Hy4’s offensive cybersecurity capabilities in the areas evaluated. Biosafety : Based on internal expert reviews, Hy4 demonstrates strong foundational biological knowledge; however, its capabilities in open-ended experimental design are more limited compared to frontier models. Delivering Greater Cost Performance, Hy4 Flash Recently Released Hy4 is currently available across Tencent Cloud TokenHub, WorkBuddy, CodeBuddy, Yuanbao, WeCom’s AI Assistant (Dayuan), ima, and more. Additionally, the model’s API is being made available via third-party platforms such as OpenRouter, Hermes, and OpenCode. Integration efforts are underway for other Tencent products and platforms, including QQ, Honor of Kings, Game of Peace, WeRead, and Tencent News. Guided by a core commitment to practical AI, Hy4 continues to push the boundaries of AI performance while delivering exceptional cost-effectiveness.

item.title: ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
item.abstract: Back to Articles ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation Enterprise Article Published November 6, 2026 Upvote 1 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai 💻 Code | 📊 Data | 🤖 Models | 📖 Documentation Robots are learning to fold laundry, sort parts, and handle unfamiliar objects. But those demonstrations are often rather narrow and don't explain what a robot has learned or why it fails. To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure. Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control. Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks : an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking. ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations, which are recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation, without requiring time-consuming teleoperation, in which a person remotely controls the robot. Researchers can easily vary these training experiences. For example, a team could generate more pushing or flipping demonstrations, then evaluate performance on tasks kept out of training. Starting with ToyBlocks as our first FoundationWorld, we aim to extend the approach to increasingly complex environments. How ToyBlocks works Building on our earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2 , MolmoBot , and MolmoSpaces , ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain. As a FoundationWorld, ToyBlocks is designed around four requirements: (1) realistic physics and appearance, (2) automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale, (3) challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity, and (4) broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain. Open-ended domains require modeling a wide range of objects and interactions, making it infeasible to fulfill all these requirements. ToyBlocks’ narrow scope, on the other hand, makes it possible to fulfill them all. Within ToyBlocks' smaller setting, researchers can work toward investigating how a robot can learn to perform any reasonable task while being confident that the simulated arm and blocks behave very similarly to their physical counterparts. A physical robot gripper above wooden blocks in the ToyBlocks setup. ToyBlocks is not just about picking and stacking blocks: pictures and letters on the blocks' faces allow for searching, sorting, and arranging tasks. A robot may need to turn a block to see a hidden face before deciding where it belongs. Domain randomization – varying block size, table height, and other physical properties from scene to scene – tests how well models generalize as the geometry changes. ToyBlocks automatically generates skills (behaviors for short tasks) and task demonstrations that can be used to train models or adapt previously trained models through additional training (fine-tuning). High-level reasoning models decide what to do; low-level action models control the robot’s movements. The framework can also be used to easily design experiments and validate hypotheses. ToyBlocks uses reinforcement learning (RL) and motion planning, which computes how the robot should move, to generate skills for short-horizon tasks, which involve brief sequences of actions. Skill training takes place in Isaac Lab, Nvidia's open-source framework for robot learning in simulation. Through trial and error, these policies – models that choose the robot’s actions – learn non-prehensile skills such as pushing a block across the table or flipping it onto another face without picking it up. Skill generation can draw on privileged information – values the simulator can supply directly but a real robot cannot, such as a block's exact position and orientation – instead of estimating it from camera images. This enables the automatic generation of skills that would require teleoperation in the real world. To generate demonstration data, a task-and-motion planner (TAMP) automatically selects and sequences the skills needed to solve a task and plans the robot’s movements between them. Running each plan in simulation produces a dataset of recorded demonstrations along with labels describing which task or skill the robot performs. ToyBlocks scales data generation through generating and executing hundreds of such plans in parallel on a single graphics processing unit (GPU), reaching up to 24 times real-time performance. Acting from sensor observations adds a perception problem: a model has to estimate a block’s pose – its position and orientation – which the simulator could supply directly. To reflect real-world conditions, ToyBlocks trains models that map raw sensor observations to actions. Execution of Molmo 2 (a high-level model) and ManiFlow (a low-level model) trained in ToyBlocks. Molmo 2 selects skills such as rotation and flipping, indicating the relevant block via a pointing interface, while ManiFlow controls the simulated arm to execute the commanded skills. ToyBlocks' controllable data generator lets users create training mixtures that emphasize particular skills or fill gaps in existing datasets. Researchers can study how much data a model needs and which experiences help it generalize to unseen tasks. For example, they could test whether adding rotation and pick-and-place demonstrations improves flipping, or vary the balance of examples inside and outside a defined workspace region—evaluating their choices on tasks kept out of training. Importantly, evaluation of trained models generates metrics beyond success rates; it provides information such as execution speeds, forces exerted on objects, and task progress measured via the same specifications used by the planning module. A webpage interface lets users connect Claude – or another frontier model – and use natural language to instruct the robot or try tasks, offering a way to explore how a model plans and acts without needing robotics expertise. Research building on ToyBlocks The evaluations below use ToyBlocks to study how training data and methods affect performance, spatial reasoning, generalization to new letters and block appearances, multi-step planning, transfer to physical robots, and frontier models that act through tools. Users can easily design their own tasks and measures to investigate other questions—for example, whether a model performs better when it selects objects by pointing or by issuing text commands such as "pick the yellow block." Low-level action models: VLA spatial generalization Low-level action models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs), map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions. The premise of VLAs is that, by pretraining on large-scale datasets, they can rapidly generalize to different scenarios or a specific workspace. However, evidence on how well these action models generalize remains conflicting. Some studies report that these action models are brittle to changes in inputs, such as different object layouts and lighting, whereas others show that VLAs generalize well.

item.title: Extend Claude Code to remote sessions on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with security controls
item.abstract: You might already run Claude Code locally on your laptop, backed by Amazon Bedrock. This post shows how to go a step further: run it as a remote agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The sample uses AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, so every task runs in its own isolated session inside your AWS account. You offload a coding task, close the laptop, and come back to the result. We first discuss why teams choose Amazon Bedrock for Claude Code and highlight a few key security characteristics. Then, we discuss the remote agent architecture and walk through an accompanying sample, sample-remote-coding-agent , that implements it. The sample runs each task in its own AgentCore runtime session and returns a GitHub pull request for you to review and merge. Along the way, we show how the Amazon Bedrock data controls stay intact when a task runs remotely. Customers choose Amazon Bedrock as Claude Code’s model provider for many reasons. These include billing and credits through their existing AWS account with no per-seat licenses, audit logging in AWS CloudTrail, and geographic inference profiles for data residency. Amazon Bedrock also provides three valuable security characteristics: Remote coding agents have become a common pattern because they turn a coding task into a hand-off. You assign the task, close the laptop or move on to other work, and come back to the result. Several tasks can run at once instead of competing for one machine, and each task runs in its own disposable environment, outside of your laptop and the credentials in your shell. The result comes back as a pull request that a teammate can review like any other change. The pattern has trade-offs: you steer less while a task runs, the environment needs some setup, and cost is harder to predict. The solution in this post runs the work in your own AWS account. Every task runs as an AgentCore runtime session that belongs to your account, and every model call goes to Amazon Bedrock, so those calls inherit the security characteristics described in the previous section. The sample suits some tasks better than others: The following diagram shows how a task flows from Claude Code or the web console through the control plane to an isolated AgentCore runtime session in your VPC, and back out as a GitHub pull request. Figure 1: Architecture of the sample The workflow consists of the following steps: Figure 2 shows the same steps as a flow. It makes two things easier to see: review can send a task back to planning, and every step reports its status to DynamoDB, which is how Claude Code and the console follow a task after you hand it off. Figure 2: How a task moves from Claude Code through an isolated AgentCore runtime session to a pull request. Numbers match the workflow steps The next section describes the security controls that the solution adds to your local setup. Running tasks remotely keeps the security characteristics of Claude Code on Amazon Bedrock for model calls and adds controls of its own. The following sections describe each control. In each session, Claude Code uses Amazon Bedrock as its only model provider. Calls go through a private Amazon Bedrock endpoint and are signed with the runtime’s IAM execution role, and the container holds no other AWS credentials. Model calls from remote tasks therefore keep the same security characteristics as Claude Code on your laptop. Each task runs in its own AgentCore runtime session, a dedicated microVM whose memory is sanitized when the session ends. AgentCore memory carries lessons from one task to later tasks on the same repository. The agent never holds a long-lived GitHub credential. The sample creates one GitHub App with read and write access to Contents and Pull requests and registers it with AgentCore Identity, which keeps the app’s client secret in its token vault. You install the app only on the repositories the agent can change and authorize each one once through three-legged OAuth (3LO). After that, each container gets a user-to-server token from Identity that expires after 8 hours and is refreshed automatically. The token reaches only repositories where the app is installed and the authorizing user has access, and commits are authored by the app’s bot account. Before a task is queued, the API screens its prompt with an Amazon Bedrock Guardrails guardrail through the ApplyGuardrail API. The guardrail uses the Standard tier, whose filters understand code. At low strength, it’s configured to block jailbreak and prompt injection attempts and misconduct, such as a request for malware. It’s also configured to block AWS access keys and other secrets. A blocked prompt returns PromptBlockedByGuardrail , and if the guardrail can’t respond, the task is refused. The guardrail screens what you type, not what the agent reads during a run, so it doesn’t see prompt injection that arrives through repository files or command output. Screening every model call would re-evaluate the full context on each call, billed by text volume, and would flag Claude Code’s own system prompt as a prompt injection attempt. Each AgentCore runtime runs in private subnets of a VPC in your AWS account, with VPC endpoints for the AWS services it calls, so the prompts, task state, and logs that it sends to those services don’t cross the internet. The only route to the internet is a NAT gateway for GitHub and package registries, and the security group allows only outbound HTTPS. An Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall blocks the model vendor’s own domains, such as api.anthropic.com , but as a denylist it doesn’t stop other HTTPS traffic. For production, consider an AWS Network Firewall domain allowlist. The AgentCore runtime IAM role can invoke only Anthropic models on Amazon Bedrock, read and write only its own repository’s task records and memory, and pull only the agent image. It’s explicitly denied the AgentCore Identity control plane, so a task can’t change the GitHub credential provider that every repository shares. The agent opens pull requests but never merges them. Turn on branch protection for the default branch so that every change gets a review. The rest of this post walks through deploying the sample in your own AWS account. You deploy the stacks, connect GitHub and register a repository, run a coding task from the web console or Claude Code, and review the pull request that it opens. Deployment takes 15–25 minutes, and registering a repository takes another 8–12 minutes. Before you begin, make sure that you have the following: The deployment bills while idle, through the NAT gateway, the interface endpoints, AWS WAF, the Cognito user pool, the DNS Firewall, images, and logs. Deploy sets a default $200 monthly Amazon Bedrock budget, which emails you but doesn’t cap spending. The sample publishes no cost estimate, so follow Clean up when you’re done. Set the AWS profile and Region in the shell you deploy from: Clone the repository, set it up, and run the read-only preflight check: Preflight prints the account and Region it deploys to and checks that AgentCore and the Claude models are available there. Confirm both before you continue. If it prints an AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) bootstrap command, run it, then run make preflight again. Part of the deployment always goes to us-east-1 , so if you deploy to another Region, bootstrap us-east-1 as well: Then deploy. It starts spending without asking you to confirm: Deploy takes 15–25 minutes, mostly for the local image build, and prints the console URL when it finishes. If it reports that the cloned repository wasn’t registered, that’s expected. You register your own repository next. Open the console URL and sign in with the temporary password that Amazon Cognito emails to you (check your spam folder), then change it. The console walks you through setup the first time you sign in.

item.title: How Greenlight Financial built an autonomous SOC solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.abstract: Greenlight Financial resolves more than 90 percent of up to 4,000 security and risk cases each month without human intervention. Greenlight’s Luna uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , infrastructure for building, connecting, and optimizing agents at scale. Specifically, Greenlight uses AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to host Luna’s agent code. It uses AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to support its tiered multi-agent system. This avoids the need to build and operate these capabilities in-house. Luna triages dark web breach-card alerts, identity anomalies, and financial-risk events in seconds. This post explains how Greenlight Financial built an autonomous security operations center (SOC) solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We cover its multi-tiered supervisor architecture, more than 30 specialized agents, episodic memory for continuous learning, and expansion from SOC use cases into financial risk triage. We share production metrics, infrastructure decisions, and patterns for building autonomous security operations in regulated industries. Greenlight Financial provides financial products for families: debit cards, savings tools, and connected devices such as the Family Hub and Pet Tracker. The company processes sensitive financial data at scale under the same regulatory requirements as major banks. Greenlight’s SOC receives 3,000–4,000 security and risk alerts per month from four primary vectors: Each alert demands cross-referencing multiple data sources before an analyst can render a verdict. A single dark web breach card notification requires checking whether the card is active, deduplicating against prior notifications, reviewing customer session data, and checking open support tickets. This workflow takes a human analyst 15-30 minutes per case. At 4,000 cases per month, that math breaks. Greenlight needed a system that could: Greenlight built Luna as a hierarchical multi-agent system on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The architecture follows a tiered supervisor pattern that mirrors how human SOC teams operate. L1 handles volume, and L2 handles complexity. Figure 1: Luna’s tiered supervisor architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Tier 1 supervisor uses an advanced language model available through Amazon Bedrock running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime within an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC). The runtime uses private subnets and direct code deployment through a ZIP file and Amazon Simple Storage Service ( Amazon S3 ). It handles initial triage of incoming cases by orchestrating more than 30 specialized agents: The Tier 1 supervisor receives cases through two paths: Amazon API Gateway, which exposes the Luna Queue API and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint, and Tines SOAR for automated alert ingestion. It determines which specialized agents to invoke based on alert type, synthesizes their findings, and renders a verdict. The median triage time for routine cases is single-digit seconds. Cases that exceed Tier 1’s confidence threshold escalate to a Tier 2 supervisor using an advanced foundation model on Amazon Bedrock with extended reasoning capabilities. This agent handles the 10 percent of cases that require multi-step reasoning: The Tier 2 supervisor runs on a scheduled basis, using Amazon EventBridge rate triggers and Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) queue completions to batch-process escalated cases, and on demand for urgent Tier 1-escalated cases. Different teams engage Luna in different ways, so the application exposes three entry points. These range from fully automated alert ingestion to interactive, on-demand investigation. Each entry point maps to a persona and how their work arrives: The memory layer is built on AgentCore memory. This layer is what separates Luna from a stateless triage tool. It supports pattern recognition, deduplication, and continuous accuracy improvement. Stores recent events and resolution outcomes. When a new alert arrives, Luna checks: “Have I seen this pattern in the last 30 days? What was the verdict? Is this a known behavior that I should allowlist?” Concrete example: A Greenlight infrastructure role generates a specific access pattern every Tuesday at 3 AM for scheduled maintenance. Without memory, Luna would flag this every week. With episodic memory, Luna learned after the first resolution that this pattern is expected and auto-allowlists it. Persists semantic preferences and resolution templates beyond the 30-day window: A dedicated pipeline feeds resolution outcomes back into the system: This pipeline drove Luna’s autonomous resolution rate from 83 percent (Tier 1 only) to more than 90 percent (Tier 1, Tier 2, and learnings). Greenlight expanded Luna into financial risk assessment within two months of the SOC deployment. The architectural changes were minimal: new specialized agents and a risk-domain supervisor layered onto the existing infrastructure. When a Greenlight customer card appears on the dark web, Luna executes this workflow autonomously: Greenlight receives hundreds of breach card notifications daily. Luna processes each in seconds. A human analyst doing the same work, logging into Galileo, checking DynamoDB, opening Mixpanel, searching Zendesk, takes 15-30 minutes per card. The following table tracks Greenlight’s security operations on the metrics that matter most to the SOC. It compares three stages: manual triage before Luna, Tier 1 automation, and the full Tier 1 and Tier 2 system. Estimated analyst time avoided: Based on Greenlight’s case volume and manual handling-time measurements, processing 4,000 cases at 15–30 minutes each would require approximately 1,000–2,000 analyst hours per month. Greenlight reports that Luna autonomously resolves more than 90 percent of these cases, avoiding an estimated 900–1,800 hours of routine manual work each month. Analysts can focus instead on cases that require human judgment. The risk reduction comes from two factors: speed (seconds compared to minutes reduces the exposure window) and consistency (Luna applies the same triage logic at 3 AM on Saturday that it does at 10 AM on Tuesday, with no fatigue and no shortcuts). Building Luna and expanding it from security operations into financial risk surfaced five lessons for teams building multi-agent systems in regulated environments: Greenlight started with security triage because the success criteria were clear: resolve the case correctly or escalate. After the pattern proved reliable at 83 percent resolution, expanding financial risk required adding new specialized agents and a risk-domain supervisor, not rebuilding the architecture. The Tier 1/Tier 2 pattern maps directly to how SOC teams already operate. L1 analysts handle volume with playbooks. L2 analysts handle the complex cases with investigation skills. This made trust-building with the security team faster. They understood the model intuitively because it matched their own escalation logic. The episodic and long-term memory layer is what moved Luna from 83 percent to more than 90 percent. Each resolved case teaches Luna something: a new allowlisted pattern, a confirmed false positive source, a resolution template. After 6 months of operation, Luna has accumulated institutional knowledge that would take a new human analyst months to build. In a regulated environment, Greenlight designed Luna to triage and recommend, not to take autonomous remediation actions without explicit policy approval. The risk expansion follows the same principle. Luna provides evidence supporting its recommendation. In this human-in-the-loop model, a human analyst or an approved automated policy authorizes and executes remediation. This separation satisfied Greenlight’s compliance requirements and built trust with the risk team.

The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and acts for signed-in users through Okta Cross App Access (XAA). Okta decided which agent might act for which user, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeemed Okta’s grant inside the agent. That proves the governance mechanism, and it runs on a deliberately small topology: one agent, two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and the authorization check written into each server. The mechanism scales. The topology doesn’t. Three things that are fine for one agent and two tools become the work in an enterprise with hundreds of agents and thousands of tools: In this post, you make that change on the Part 1 solution. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, becomes the single front door and redeems Okta’s grant for each target. Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore evaluates Cedar policies that bind each tool to the agent and the scope Okta delegated. A second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) joins under its own Okta identity, to show that the front door doesn’t care where an agent runs. And Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Amazon CloudWatch gives you one place to read every decision, including Okta’s. We also compare XAA with per-user OAuth consent for applications that can’t accept Okta’s grant. The Okta configuration, the AgentCore Identity credential provider, and the MCP servers from Part 1 stay as they are. Figure 1 shows the architecture with the additions. Figure 1: The Part 1 solution with AgentCore Gateway, Policy, and Observability, a second agent on Amazon EKS, and the audit path, with numbers matching the steps that follow The reporting agent, agent B, runs on Amazon EKS and follows the same path through its own Gateway. In addition to the Part 1 solution, you need the following: The additions take about 90 minutes. The EKS control plane costs $0.10 per hour, plus nodes and the Amazon EKS Auto Mode management fee, and the AgentCore features charge for what you use. See Amazon EKS pricing and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing . As in Part 1, the base for this solution is the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain on GitHub, and you can build the Part 2 additions on top of it. Beyond that sample, the snippets and configurations in this post show the pattern conceptually. They aren’t a complete, deployable solution. The code is sample code for non-production use, so work with your security and legal teams to meet your organization’s security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before you deploy it. The Gateway’s inbound authorizer works like the runtime authorizer from Part 1. Its issuer is Okta’s org authorization server, its audience is the custom authorization server, and allowedClients pins it to one agent: Figure 2 shows the resulting inbound authorizer. Figure 2: The Gateway accepts only ID-JAGs that Okta issued to the agent for the resource’s authorization server Each MCP server becomes a Gateway target whose outbound authorization uses TOKEN_EXCHANGE through the Part 1 credential provider, so the Gateway performs the second exchange: Figure 3 shows a target configured this way. Figure 3: The task manager target redeems the ID-JAG through the Part 1 credential provider Three details matter here. First, as in Part 1, the target’s scopes must equal the ID-JAG’s. Second, give each target a static tool schema ( listingMode set to DEFAULT with an inline mcpToolSchema ), so the tool names your Cedar policies reference are fixed when you write them. In our tests, policies that name tools also couldn’t attach to dynamically listed targets. Third, the Gateway pages tools/list by target, so your client must follow the pagination cursor, or tools from later targets disappear. AgentCore Identity keeps the token from the Gateway’s exchange, so one single-use ID-JAG serves every tool call in a session. In our tests, it also opened a second session within its 5-minute life. Because a credential provider authenticates as one Okta agent, give each agent its own Gateway and provider. Sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain takes a different route, in which a Gateway interceptor performs both exchanges itself. Attach a Policy in AgentCore engine to the Gateway in ENFORCE mode, and write permit-only policies. Cedar exposes JWT claims as tags. A policy that reads a missing tag errors and is skipped. A skipped permit grants nothing, so default deny holds, but a skipped forbid blocks nothing. Guard each tag with hasTag : The scope tag holds the ID-JAG’s space-separated scope claim, so the four conditions match xaa:write only as a whole entry. A scope such as xaa:write-admin doesn’t match. A matching policy, written the same way, permits the read tools with xaa:read . Check that every policy is ACTIVE before you attach the engine: an engine whose policies failed to create leaves the Gateway denying every call. Cedar binds tools to the agent and its delegated scope, and the MCP server still decides each user’s authority from the groups claim, as in Part 1. Agent A now forwards its inbound ID-JAG to the Gateway instead of calling AgentCore Identity itself: Remove the Part 1 AgentCore Identity statements from the agent’s execution role. That’s the only change to the role, which now holds no token-exchange or secret permissions, because the Gateway’s role holds the permission to exchange tokens. Keep allowedClients on the runtime’s authorizer. Our second agent, a reporting agent, runs the same code on Amazon EKS with its own Okta registration. Its resource connection allows only xaa:read , and it has its own Gateway and credential provider. EKS Pod Identity gives the pod an IAM role that can invoke models and write its own logs and traces, and nothing else. The AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) SDK exports its traces. The agents-on-eks sample shows the Pod Identity setup. Outside AgentCore runtime, no authorizer sits in front of the pod, so the agent validates the ID-JAG before a model call. It checks the signature, issuer, audience, token type oauth-id-jag+jwt , expiry, and that client_id is its own. If you kept the Part 1 agent check in the MCP servers, add agent B’s client ID to REGISTERED_AGENTS . Two settings tripped us up. The EKS Auto Mode general-purpose node pool runs only amd64, so build multi-architecture images. And the AgentCore Python SDK, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, binds to localhost unless you set DOCKER_CONTAINER=true . The spans in this section are AgentCore Observability , the component in Figure 1 that sits between the agents and CloudWatch. Runtime, Gateway, Identity, and Policy emit OpenTelemetry spans for each hop without code changes, after you turn on Transaction Search and trace delivery. Your own services add theirs with the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT). CloudWatch Transaction Search collects them, the AgentCore console reads them as agent traces, and Amazon CloudWatch Omni reads the same spans as traces.default , which is what lets one query put them beside Okta’s events. One tool call therefore produces this chain of spans, each naming the control that made a decision: Okta’s System Log is the one record AWS can’t emit, so you bring it in. Figure 4 shows both paths meeting in Omni. Figure 4: The audit path, where spans and Okta’s System Log reach CloudWatch and one Omni query joins them One query then joins each ID-JAG grant to the decisions it led to: For Alice, the result shows Okta granting the task agent xaa:read xaa:write for her, then the MCP server denying her create_task 16.7 seconds later and allowing list_tasks after that, as Figure 5 shows.

item.title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 1
item.abstract: An AI agent that updates a ticket or reads a customer record acts for a person, inside applications that person can reach. Your identity team then has to answer a question that per-app OAuth consent and shared service accounts leave open: which agent might act for which user in which application, and how you stop it. Okta Cross App Access (XAA) answers it in your identity provider (IdP). You register the agent in Okta, an administrator approves the applications it might reach, and Okta evaluates policy each time the agent asks to act for a user. In our tests, after an administrator removed a user’s assignment to the agent, Okta refused the agent’s new requests for that user within about 1 second, and tokens already issued expired within 5 minutes. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This solution uses two of its capabilities to carry out Okta’s decision on AWS. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, validates Okta’s grant. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeems it for a short-lived access token with credentials your agent code doesn’t see, and keeps that token in its token vault. In our tests, AgentCore Identity added about 0.6 seconds to a request that took about 30 seconds end to end. In this post, the first of two, you build a task agent on AgentCore runtime that acts for signed-in users through XAA and AgentCore Identity. You configure the AgentCore Identity parts it needs, enforce each user’s authority in the tools, and see what we measured: what each check refuses, the practices we settled on, and how fast Okta’s controls take effect. Part 2 then puts the same governance behind Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Cedar policies, a second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), and an audit trail in Amazon CloudWatch. Okta is the governance plane: it decides which agent might act for which user, against which resource. AgentCore Identity is the execution plane: it holds the agent’s credentials, turns Okta’s decision into a token the resource accepts, and keeps both identities in that token. In Figure 1, the agent and the two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers it calls all run on AgentCore runtime. Figure 1: Solution architecture, with numbers matching the steps that follow Each request carries three tokens, and each records a different decision: the ID token says who the user is, the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) is Okta’s decision, and the access token is what the resource accepts. One request flows like this: Figure 2 shows the same request as a sequence, with the check that each party makes. Figure 2: The three-token chain and the check each party makes, with the step 4 workload access token staying inside AWS To follow along, you need the following: The walkthrough takes about 1 hour. AgentCore charges for what you use. See Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing . The base for this solution is the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain in the AgentCore samples repository on GitHub, and you can build the solution in this post on top of it. Beyond that sample, the snippets and configurations in this post show the pattern conceptually. They aren’t a complete, deployable solution. The code is sample code for non-production use, so work with your security and legal teams to meet your organization’s security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before you deploy it. Okta needs an authorization server for the resource, the agent, a connection between them, and a policy that admits the agent’s grant. Do all of these steps in the Okta Admin Console: registering the agent creates its linked app, so you don’t need an app integration wizard. Figure 3: The task agent’s resource connection in Okta, limited to the xaa:read and xaa:write scopes Okta’s Cross App Access guide covers the console steps, and the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain scripts the authorization server and its JWT bearer policy. The BFF then requests the ID-JAG, authenticated as the agent: The AWS sample 06-okta-xaa sends the same request in Python ( agent/xaa_client.py ). The BFF authenticates as the agent, so store the agent’s client secret in AWS Secrets Manager rather than in code or configuration files. AgentCore Identity holds three things for this solution, and your agent code doesn’t see the client secret or call Okta’s token endpoint: The credential provider performs the second exchange. Point it at the custom authorization server, authenticate it as the AI agent, and set the on-behalf-of grant to JWT_AUTHORIZATION_GRANT , which AgentCore Identity sends as jwt-bearer with the ID-JAG as the assertion: Okta binds both exchanges to the client named in the ID-JAG, so each Okta agent needs its own provider: when we redeemed one agent’s ID-JAG as another, Okta refused with “The ‘client_id’ in the JWT Bearer Grant must match the ‘client_id’ used to authenticate the client.” AgentCore Identity keeps the secret in a service-managed AWS Secrets Manager secret, which you rotate with update-oauth2-credential-provider . If your team already manages the client secret in Secrets Manager, you can reference that secret’s ARN instead. AgentCore Identity reads the client secret from it, so you can rotate the secret without updating the provider (see Reference your own AWS Secrets Manager secrets in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity ). To avoid a shared secret, authenticate with a private key instead. See Authenticate with Private Key JWT using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity . Figure 4 shows the provider in the AgentCore console. Figure 4: The credential provider authenticating as the agent with the JWT authorization grant AgentCore runtime creates and manages a workload identity for each agent runtime. When a request passes the runtime’s JWT authorizer, the runtime gets a workload access token for that workload identity and the inbound token’s issuer and subject, and passes it to your code. AgentCore Identity then uses the ID-JAG behind it as the assertion for the exchange. The AgentCore Python SDK keeps the workload access token in BedrockAgentCoreContext , not in the request headers that your entrypoint receives. Our first version looked for it in the headers, found nothing, and fell back to its own GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT call with a second workload identity, on all 21 requests we checked. Read it from the context instead: AgentCore Identity keeps the access token in its token vault for the rest of the request. Across 10 requests, the agent’s first call redeemed the ID-JAG in about half a second (see the latency table in Validate the results), and the second, for the other MCP server, returned the same token in a median of 58 milliseconds without redeeming the single-use ID-JAG again. A new ID-JAG for the same user got a new token, so each request reflects Okta’s latest decision. The sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain reads the workload access token the same way ( agent/agent.py ). AgentCore Identity doesn’t bind workload identities to credential providers in the same account. The agent’s IAM role does, so scope it to the agent’s own workload identity and provider, and to that provider’s secret: Take the workload identity’s name from workloadIdentityDetails in GetAgentRuntime , and the provider’s ARN from credentialProviderArn : the segment is oauth2credentialprovider , and with the hyphenated form every call failed with AccessDeniedException . The role needs no GetWorkloadAccessToken permission, because the runtime gets that token, not the agent. Our tests passed with only these two statements. Configure the agent runtime’s inbound authorizer to accept only ID-JAGs that Okta issued to this agent. Its issuer is Okta’s org authorization server, and its audience is the resource’s custom authorization server. In agentcore.

item.title: How to Give Your AI Agent Memory
item.abstract: How to Give Your AI Agent Memory Learn how to give AI agents long-term memory using the OpenAI Agents SDK, Mem0, and MCP to remember preferences, context, and important information across sessions. By Abid Ali Awan , KDnuggets Assistant Editor on November 6, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence AI agents can reason, use tools, and complete complex tasks. But there is one problem: most of them forget everything once the session ends. That means every new conversation can feel like starting from scratch. Agent memory gives an AI system a way to remember useful information across sessions , such as your preferences, previous decisions, goals, or important context. In this tutorial, we will build an AI agent with long-term memory using the OpenAI Agents SDK and Mem0 . We will then connect the same memory system to OpenCode so your coding agent can remember information across sessions too. How AI Agent Memory Works A simple agent memory system follows a straightforward loop: the user sends a message, the agent searches its memory for relevant context, uses that information while reasoning, and then saves anything useful for future conversations. There are two main types of memory: Short-term memory: Information from the current conversation or task, such as recent messages and temporary state. Long-term memory: Information that persists across sessions, such as preferences, decisions, goals, and previous experiences. The key part is retrieval . Instead of adding every previous conversation to the prompt, the agent searches its memory and brings back only the information that is relevant to the current request. This keeps the context smaller while still allowing the agent to behave as if it remembers previous interactions. Building an Agent with Long-Term Memory In this section, we will build a simple agent that can search, save, and reuse information across conversations. Start by installing the OpenAI Agents SDK and Mem0: pip install openai-agents mem0ai Next, set the API keys: export OPENAI_API_KEY="your-openai-key" export MEM0_API_KEY="your-mem0-key" Then import the required classes and create a Mem0 client: from agents import Agent, Runner, function_tool from mem0 import MemoryClient memory = MemoryClient() USER_ID = "abid" The MemoryClient gives our agent access to Mem0, while USER_ID tells Mem0 whose memories to store and retrieve. Using a separate identifier for each user keeps their memory isolated. Creating a Memory Search Tool Now we need to give the agent a way to look up relevant information from previous conversations. We do this by creating a search_memory tool that sends the current query to Mem0 and returns the most relevant stored memories. @function_tool def search_memory(query: str) -> str: """Search for relevant memories about the user.""" results = memory.search( query=query, filters={"user_id": USER_ID}, top_k=5, ) memories = results.get("results", []) if not memories: return "No relevant memories found." return "\n".join( f"- {item['memory']}" for item in memories ) Mem0 uses semantic search, so the wording does not have to match exactly. As long as the meaning is similar, the agent can still retrieve the right memory. Creating a Memory Writing Tool Next, we need a way for the agent to save useful information for future conversations. We do this with a save_memory tool that sends important facts, preferences, or decisions to Mem0. @function_tool def save_memory(content: str) -> str: """Save useful long-term information about the user.""" memory.add( messages=[ { "role": "user", "content": content, } ], user_id=USER_ID, ) return "Memory saved." Mem0 can then process that information and store the parts that are useful as long-term memory, rather than saving the entire conversation as one large block. Creating the Agent Now we can connect everything by creating the agent and giving it access to both memory tools. The agent is instructed to check for relevant memories before answering and to save useful information that should be remembered later. agent = Agent( name="Memory Assistant", model="gpt-5.6-luna", instructions=""" You are a personal assistant with long-term memory. Always call search_memory before answering, even for general questions. When a relevant memory is found, acknowledge it naturally at the start, for example: "Oh, I remember you prefer...", then use it. Save durable preferences, goals, and facts; confirm each save in one sentence. Skip greetings, temporary info, and duplicates. """, tools=[ search_memory, save_memory, ], ) Here, the instructions control how the agent uses memory. They tell it what to retrieve, what to save, and what kinds of information should be ignored. Finally, create a small chat() function to run the agent: def chat(message): result = Runner.run_sync( agent, message, ) return result.final_output Each time chat() is called, the message is passed to the agent, which can use the memory tools as part of its response. Testing the Memory Now let's check that the agent can actually remember something across interactions. First, give it a preference worth saving: print(chat( "Remember that I prefer Python and use uv " "for managing my projects." )) Output: I'll remember that you prefer Python and use `uv` to manage your projects. Next, ask a related question: print(chat( "How should I set up my next Python project?" )) Output: I remember you prefer Python and use **uv** for project management. A solid setup: ```bash uv init my-project cd my-project uv add <runtime-dependency> uv add --dev pytest ruff mypy ``` The agent can retrieve the saved preference with search_memory() and use it to make the response more relevant. Because the memory is stored in Mem0, it can still be retrieved even after the Python application is restarted. Giving OpenCode the Same Memory We can also give a coding agent such as OpenCode persistent memory without writing the Python tools ourselves. Mem0 provides an official hosted Model Context Protocol (MCP) server with tools for adding, searching, updating, and deleting memories. Add it to OpenCode with: npx mcp-add \ --name mem0-mcp \ --type http \ --url "https://mcp.mem0.ai/mcp" \ --clients "opencode" Restart OpenCode and test it: Remember that I prefer uv instead of pip for new Python projects. Then start a new session and ask: How should I initialize this Python project? OpenCode can retrieve the stored preference through the Mem0 MCP tools. Mem0 currently exposes operations including add_memory , search_memories , get_memories , update_memory , delete_memory , and more. You can verify the connection with: opencode mcp list Final Thoughts ChatGPT has a memory feature that can remember useful information from previous conversations and bring it back in later sessions. That is why it can sometimes feel like ChatGPT already understands what you are trying to say without you having to explain everything again. You can create a similar experience in your own AI applications. For example, you can build an assistant that remembers customer preferences, an internal tool that keeps track of important decisions, or a coding agent that remembers your preferred frameworks, project rules, and development habits. The main benefit is that users do not have to start from scratch every time. The agent can retrieve relevant information from earlier sessions and use it to give more personalized and consistent responses. In this guide, we learned how AI agent memory works, how short-term and long-term memory differ, and how to use Mem0 with the OpenAI Agents SDK to save and retrieve memories. We also connected the same memory system to OpenCode through MCP. Abid Ali Awan ( @1abidaliawan ) is a certified data scientist professional who loves building machine learning models. Currently, he is focusing on content creation and writing technical blogs on machine learning and data science technologies.
