item.title: Serverless MCP server for AI agent data lake access on Amazon ECS Fargate
item.abstract: Organizations building applications powered by artificial intelligence (AI) face a recurring challenge: giving large language model (LLM) agents access to enterprise data lakes without duplicating integration logic across every agent and application. Most teams begin by wiring agents directly to databases and APIs, with no shared gateway such as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in between. Each new dataset demands custom code, and each agent reimplements its own access control. As the number of datasets or agents grows, permission enforcement drifts, and onboarding a new data source becomes a multi-day engineering effort. Our team supports Amazon’s North America Sort Center (NASC) network, where planning teams rely on operational data to manage capacity, labor, and package flow. To give those teams conversational access to that data, we built a serverless Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate to address this problem for planning teams in NASC. The server acts as a centralized, agent-agnostic gateway between AI agents and our enterprise data lake. Exposing a new dataset requires only a JSON metadata file that the server discovers automatically on the next pipeline sync. In this post, we describe the architecture, show how a metadata-driven approach removes the need for per-dataset integration code, and explain how the serverless infrastructure supports multiple agents and applications in a multi-tenant environment. Two interrelated challenges shaped how we designed this system: fragmented data access patterns and an unsustainable onboarding model. Our data lake contains thousands of datasets spanning operational metrics, business analytics, and domain-specific data. Multiple teams wanted AI assistants that could query this data conversationally, but each built its own integration from scratch. Each agent embedded its own SQL generation logic, schema knowledge, and connection handling, so a schema change meant patching every agent individually. Access control was fragmented, with no single audit point for data access decisions. Onboarding a new dataset required custom tool code, query validation, and redeployment, typically a multi-day effort per table. We established four requirements: The architecture separates concerns into four layers (client, MCP server, tools, and knowledge-base refresh), each independently scalable and deployable. A metadata catalog underpins the tools layer, storing schema descriptions, column-level semantics, and table relationships that the AI agent references when generating SQL. Because the agent derives schema knowledge from the catalog at query time, there is no need to hardcode table structures or redeploy when schemas change. The knowledge-base refresh layer keeps that catalog current, indexing new dataset metadata as it arrives. The following sections describe each layer in detail. The following diagram shows the request flow from user query to data layer across all four layers. A user submits a query from a client application (web chat, Slack, an IDE plugin, or an external agent). The request resolves through Amazon Route 53 for DNS and reaches an Application Load Balancer in a public subnet, configured with HTTPS and AWS WAF. The load balancer routes to Amazon Cognito, which authenticates the user and enriches the request. Authenticated traffic then enters the private subnet, where the client layer runs on Amazon ECS Fargate. This layer handles session state in Amazon DynamoDB and forwards requests through an internal Application Load Balancer to the MCP server layer, also on Amazon ECS Fargate. In the MCP server layer, an AI agent powered by Amazon Bedrock orchestrates tools built with FastMCP (a Python framework for building MCP servers). Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is applied to every model interaction. On the right, the data layer holds the tool backends. Amazon Athena and Amazon Redshift run SQL queries against the data lake, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability, handles semantic search. Data ingestion into Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and the knowledge bases is handled by AWS Lambda. Each layer is described in detail in the sections that follow. Figure 1: Request flow through the serverless MCP server, from client applications to the data layer A request flows from the client application through Amazon Route 53 for DNS resolution to an Application Load Balancer configured with HTTPS and AWS WAF . The load balancer forwards traffic to the Amazon ECS Fargate client service, which integrates with Amazon Cognito for JSON Web Token (JWT) authentication and Amazon DynamoDB for session storage. A context mapping configuration drives this enrichment, scoping each query to only the relevant tables. In our testing, this scoping keeps end-to-end interaction latency in the 15–20 second range. The following example shows a context mapping configuration: When a context specifies tables, the MCP server narrows its search of the metadata catalog to those tables, reducing noise and improving SQL generation accuracy. Adding a new business domain requires only adding an entry to this mapping. The MCP server runs on its own ECS Fargate cluster, isolated from the client layer. Requests reach it through Amazon Route 53 and an internal Application Load Balancer in a private subnet. The server handles full orchestration including query analysis, tool selection, execution, and response generation. Through the MCP protocol endpoint ( /mcp ), a FastMCP-powered JSON-RPC interface, external MCP-compatible clients such as Amazon Q Developer or IDE extensions can discover and invoke tools directly. Fargate tasks are stateless with conversation state persisted in DynamoDB, so tasks can be replaced or scaled without data loss. When a request arrives, the agent retrieves session history, analyzes user intent using Amazon Bedrock, discovers and invokes appropriate tools, and streams results back to the user. Each tool is registered with FastMCP and discoverable at runtime: The Athena query tools are the primary interface to the data lake. The agent first queries the metadata catalog to understand available schemas, generates an optimized SQL query through Amazon Bedrock, validates and auto-corrects the SQL for Athena compatibility, then executes it. Results flow back to the orchestrating agent for natural language synthesis. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is applied to all LLM interactions and is designed to filter harmful content, enforce grounding checks, and help block prompt injection attempts. These guardrails operate as production controls at the MCP server layer, so every connected agent benefits from the same content safety policies regardless of how it connects. The Athena query tools enforce SELECT -only queries, rejecting write operations at the tool level before they reach the data lake. The entire system is built around configuration-driven extensibility. Adding a new dataset requires a metadata JSON file describing the table and an optional context mapping entry. The file captures the table’s schema, business context, and column-level semantics. It serves as the single source of truth that the AI agent uses to understand and query the dataset: The business_description_for_the_table field carries engine-specific query hints, such as “always use date() to wrap string literals,” that reduce SQL validation failures. The column_details field pairs each column_name [type] with a natural language description and sample values, giving the agent both schema awareness and business semantics. The sample_values field matters for accurate WHERE clause generation because the agent learns real data patterns, for instance that warehouse_id holds codes like FC-EAST-07 rather than spelled-out names like “East region facility.

item.title: Google Releases Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: 15-Second AI Video at $0.07 per Second
item.abstract: Google has released Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash , the newest version of its video generation and editing model. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates and edits clips up to 15 seconds natively. It also cuts the price by 30% compared with Omni 1.1 Flash. The model is generally available on Google Cloud and the Gemini API . For developers, the takeaways are longer clips, fewer re-renders and a lower bill per second. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is a multimodal video model from Google DeepMind. It takes text, images, short video clips and audio as input. It outputs video with audio. Google’s developer docs describe the Omni line as natively multimodal, with editing handled through the Interactions API. Google frames cost control as a workflow, not just a price. You draft at 360p or 720p. You fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of regenerating the whole clip. Then you upscale the best result to 1080p or 4K. Multi-turn conversational editing now works across full 15-second clips. In practice, you can swap a product, background, lighting or aspect ratio turn by turn. The docs show this through a previous_interaction_id , so the prior video is not re-uploaded. Google prices Omni 1.2 Flash at $0.07 per second of 720p video . Savings are similar at other resolutions . For context, the pricing page bills Omni 1.1 Flash at roughly $0.10 per second of 720p video. A full 15-second 720p clip on 1.2 works out to about $1.05. Google Vids users can generate 15-second clips at no additional cost. Provisioned Throughput is available, and outputs carry a SynthID watermark. Google has not published benchmark scores for version 1.2. Its claims rest on side-by-side demos against Omni 1.1. The DeepMind model page reports human-rater results for the Omni Flash line, including 1,003 MovieGenBench prompts. In June, an earlier Omni Flash version took #1 on the Arena text-to-video board . Those rankings predate 1.2, so treat them as family context only. Early partner feedback is positive but self-selected. item.title: Taxbit Assist: A grounded, role-aware AI agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.abstract: Taxbit is a digital-asset tax and accounting compliance platform. Founded in 2018, Taxbit helps enterprises such as exchanges, payment services, and brokers calculate gains and losses, collect tax documentation, and file information returns at scale. Now, a cited, permission-aware AI assistant helps compliance teams find answers right inside the product dashboard. But the knowledge needed to use that dashboard well was scattered across the public website, API documentation, and help-center articles, and a meaningful share was never written down at all. When a customer asked “what does this form status mean?”, they either went digging or filed a support ticket. Today more than 55 percent of users who ask Assist a question return to ask another within 24 hours, according to Taxbit’s internal production analytics. In this post, we share how we built Taxbit Assist , the AI assistant now embedded in the Taxbit dashboard, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. We cover the architecture, the retrieval work that made answers trustworthy enough to ship to regulated customers, how we handle safety and data residency, and how we continuously measure answer quality on live production traffic. A generic chatbot was not an option in this domain. Four constraints shaped what we built: We are also a small team. Rather than build and operate the agent loop, conversation-state store, and session isolation ourselves, we chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for three reasons: its managed agent runtime removed infrastructure operations, built-in AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, eliminated a separate conversation-state store, and per-session isolation kept each user’s context contained. That let us put most of our effort into the retrieval and safety work that follows. Taxbit Assist is a Strands Agents SDK application running on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The following diagram illustrates the solution architecture. Figure 1: Request flow from a dashboard question through guardrails screening, knowledge base retrieval, model reasoning, permission checks, and response streaming The workflow consists of the following steps: The agent is a small Python application: a system prompt, a model, and eight tools. It ships as an ARM64 container image that AgentCore runtime pulls from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) and scales on demand. The tools are deliberately narrow: In this version, the agent has no read access to customer tax data. It answers from product knowledge, and the only writes it can perform are the caller’s own support tickets. One security decision underpins all of them: the model never handles identity. The user’s email, organization ID, and roles come from the trusted calling service and are bound into each tool through a closure before the model sees it. The model can decide whether to check permissions but not whose permissions to check, because identity isn’t a parameter it can set. User input is sanitized at the boundary, so a prompt injection cannot imitate the trusted context line. The agent runs a foundation model (FM) through Amazon Bedrock, invoked through cross-Region inference profiles. Geography-aware inference handles data residency. The inference profile ID carries a geography prefix derived from the deployment Region, so EU deployments keep inference within the EU, and US deployments stay in the US. Beyond keeping inference in the right geography, we also support a bring your own key (BYOK) model. In BYOK accounts, conversation history and the other stores that hold client data are encrypted with the customer’s own AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key. Application inference profiles handle cost visibility. Each deployment wraps the system inference profile in a tagged application profile, so every model invocation carries cost-allocation tags and shows up in AWS Cost Explorer, broken down by workload. Amazon Bedrock prompt caching cuts latency and token cost. The system prompt is byte-identical for every request and ends with a cache checkpoint, so the static prefix is cached across users. Per-request context travels on the user message instead. Most of our engineering effort went into the knowledge base: an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base backed by Amazon S3 Vectors, with Cohere Embed English v3 for embeddings, producing 1,024-dimension float32 vectors compared by cosine distance. All of it is managed, so there is no vector database for us to operate. Content flows in from three kinds of sources, each landing under its own prefix in a single Amazon S3 bucket. The following diagram shows how content reaches the index. Figure 2: Content ingestion pipeline from published, code-derived, and curated sources through Lambda scrapers into Amazon S3 and the knowledge base Published content comes first: our public website, our API documentation, and our help-center articles, crawled by scheduled AWS Lambda functions. With sitemap lastmod timestamps and content hashes, a typical run only touches what changed since the previous one. Scoping mattered more than we anticipated. Our sitemap has roughly over 400 URLs, but only about over 70 belong in an answer-generating corpus, and /blogs/ alone accounts for more than 300 marketing pages. Left in, that campaign content competes with the help center to become the cited source for compliance questions. Excluding it was one of our highest-value retrieval changes, and it required no model work at all. The second source is less conventional: Lambda functions read our product source code and generate Markdown documentation covering dashboard routes, permission gates, form eligibility logic, and reporting configuration. This captures product truth that exists nowhere else in prose, and it stays current because it’s regenerated from the code itself. The third source is curated content: hand-written articles and approved corrections that fill gaps the automated sources don’t cover. Amazon EventBridge schedules the crawls on a staggered nightly and weekly cadence, and each scraper triggers an ingestion job only when something has changed. We group the nine scrapers into three umbrella data sources split by S3 sub-prefix (product-public/, product-internals/, curated/), which keeps related content together. We chose semantic chunking, which splits documents at natural boundaries and outperformed fixed-size chunking on our retrieval tests. But a chunk pulled from the middle of a document loses track of what the document is about. In tax reporting, that context is often the whole answer: a passage that applies only to non-US filing regimes is actively misleading if it’s returned for a question about IRS Form 1099 (an information return for reporting payments). To fix this, we used the knowledge base’s custom transformation hook to run a POST_CHUNKING Lambda function that prepends each chunk with its document’s H1 title and lead paragraph, which usually states where the content applies. The prefix is capped at roughly 128 tokens (80 characters of title and 300 of scope). Because Cohere Embed English v3 accepts up to 512 tokens per input, chunk bodies are capped at 384 so the header and body fit within that window together. A production probe found about 28 percent of our chunks sat in the 385–512 band and would have had their tails silently truncated. This was the highest-impact retrieval change we made: chunks now carry their own scope into the vector index, instead of it living only in the document’s first chunk. Two practical notes: First, Amazon Bedrock requires the transformation’s intermediate storage to be a separate bucket from the data source bucket. A distinct prefix on the same bucket is rejected. Second, enabling a custom transformation on an existing data source forces a replacement, so plan for a full re-ingestion rather than an in-place change.

item.title: Real-time fraud detection with Feature Views
item.abstract: Real-time fraud detection depends on three kinds of features: what a customer did seconds ago, how they normally spend and how the current payment compares. Those features have to be computed the same way for model training and for live scoring — otherwise data leakage and training-serving skew quietly erode model quality. Feature Views, part of Databricks Feature Store, address this. You define each feature once, and that definition produces both point-in-time training data and the managed pipelines for online inference. A $900 payment may be routine for one customer and unusual for another. When it arrives, a fraud model has only a moment to decide whether it looks normal, needs review or should be blocked. Approving a fraudulent transaction can cost the customer money. Blocking a legitimate one disrupts their payment experience and erodes their trust in the platform. The transaction alone doesn't tell the whole story. The model also needs to know how this customer normally transacts and what they did seconds, minutes, days or weeks ago. During training, features must use only information available when each payment occurred. During live scoring, they must reflect recent transactions quickly enough to catch suspicious activity. If the two paths implement the logic separately, small differences between them creep in. This walkthrough follows that $900 payment from a Kafka stream to a fraud score served by Model Serving, with code at each step. The central idea is that one feature definition, driving both training and serving, gives you point-in-time correct training data and consistent online features. You don't build a separate pipeline for each path. A Feature View is a Databricks Feature Store definition that specifies a feature's source, entity keys, time semantics and transformation. The same definition computes historical values for training and drives the managed pipelines that keep features fresh for serving. One API covers batch, streaming and on-demand features. Unity Catalog governs their definitions, permissions and lineage. Two failure modes motivate this design: Feature Views bring streaming feature computation into the same data science workflow as historical training and live scoring. You can evaluate features against past transactions, then use the same definitions to keep customer context fresh for live decisions. The goal is to flag suspicious payments as they arrive without raising false alarms on legitimate ones. On its own, the $900 payment may look harmless. But if it's the 10th payment in five minutes, it could be part of a suspicious burst. Any delay in recognizing that burst gives someone with access to a compromised account more time to make additional payments. A Fraud Detection application built with Databricks Apps processes a stream of financial transactions. Each event includes a customer ID, amount, payment type, timestamp and origin and destination countries. The application sends each transaction to a Model Serving endpoint. It then displays the transaction's risk score alongside live transaction volume, flagged transactions and country-to-country flows. The model combines three kinds of context: The architecture has a historical path for training and an online path for inference. Both start from the same feature definitions in Unity Catalog. The historical path reads the Stream's ingestion table to build point-in-time training sets. The online path materializes aggregates to the Online Feature Store, where Model Serving reads them at request time. Before deciding which features to serve, you can test alternatives against historical transactions. Does a five-minute transaction count give a stronger signal than a 15-minute count? Does comparing the current amount with the customer's spending variability help beyond using their average alone? In this example, customer transaction events arrive as Kafka streams. A registered Stream holds the connection, schema and ingestion settings, and a StreamSource references it to compute real-time features. Kafka topics don't retain enough history for model training. Databricks therefore manages an offline copy of the stream in an ingestion table. For training or backfilling an online store, Databricks calculates historical values from the ingestion table and uses the live Kafka feed for the most recent data. On ingest, transformation_sql reshapes nested fields from the Kafka value payload into the schema the features need. The projection becomes part of the source definition, so you don't deploy a separate preprocessing pipeline. For our payment, the Kafka value payload contains: The demo uses demo_user_id alongside customer_id to keep the customer histories of different app users separate. We define the five-minute count with RollingWindow . The companion notebook includes imports, configuration, and the full source projection. You can inspect its historical values in a notebook with compute_features(features=[recent_transaction_count]) . The 10-minute total uses the same source and keys, with Sum over a 10-minute RollingWindow. A Sawtooth window is a long-lookback aggregation whose oldest boundary advances in daily steps. It combines batch-computed history with streaming updates for recent activity. For our $900 payment, SawtoothWindow adds a 30-day spending baseline to the short rolling windows. Both kinds of window keep recent activity fresh. Because the Sawtooth window's oldest boundary moves daily rather than continuously, its effective lookback is slightly longer than 30 days. The baseline uses the built-in Avg , StddevPop and Count aggregations on payment amounts over the same Sawtooth window. Databricks starts a managed ingestion pipeline when a Stream is created and keeps incoming events in its ingestion table. If you also need events from before the Stream existed, StreamBackfillSource lets you supply your own history during Stream setup. Once the table covers the full lookback, a new Sawtooth feature can use it right away instead of waiting 30 days for events to accumulate. An on-demand feature is computed at request time by combining values from the scoring request with stored features. Comparing a live transaction against a customer's historical baseline is a common way to spot abnormal behavior. In Feature Views, inference-time information is represented with a RequestSource — here, transaction_amount from the application's request. Two customers can both average $300 per payment but spend very differently. With standard deviations of $100 and $600, the same $900 payment sits six standard deviations above one customer's average and only one above the other's. The model combines this comparison with recent activity and payment details to estimate fraud risk. The Sawtooth aggregations maintain the 30-day average and standard deviation. The on-demand feature combines them with the current amount to calculate (current_amount - average) / standard_deviation . We implement this calculation as a Python UDF registered in Unity Catalog: The feature definition uses registered upstream Feature objects. FeatureViewSource brings together the current amount and the three 30-day statistics, and CustomUDF invokes the function: When there isn't enough usable history, the function returns zero as a fallback. A separate indicator lets the model tell that fallback apart from a true zero, which means the payment matches the customer's average. The same derived feature is evaluated against historical inputs during training, and against the current request plus retrieved statistics during inference. During feature development, you can inspect feature definitions in a notebook with compute_features() . This works for derived features whose inputs come entirely from historical source data. For request-dependent comparisons such as amount_deviation , use create_training_set() instead, which supplies the current payment fields from labeled examples.

item.title: Taxonomy of agentic primitives in Amazon Quick
item.abstract: Over the past year, as we built Amazon Quick, our agents went from answering questions to taking actions: scheduling meetings, running research, generating reports. As the system evolved, one problem kept resurfacing: there was no shared definition of the primitives that agentic work is built from. The same few ideas kept getting rebuilt under different names: an actor that does the work, a signal that starts it, a packaged procedure, and a memory that carries lessons forward. This repetition leaked into product design and onto the user. Take the user who says “ monitor my Slack channel and send me a daily digest ”. Is that a new agent, a scheduled instruction to an existing one, a workflow, or a skill? These are different questions, but without a shared vocabulary they collapse into one confusing choice. This post shares the taxonomy we converged on: one set of primitives found by decomposing agentic work into four plain questions: When? , What? , Who? , and How? Most of the framework stays invisible to end users by design, but a shared vocabulary makes the system easier to reason about for anyone building beneath it. Figure 1: How triggers, agents, and capabilities relate, with learning feeding back from the session runtime A trigger starts the work and carries the task ( When and What ), an agent takes it on ( Who ) and uses its capabilities (tools, skills, and workflows) to perform the task ( How ). This post describes these primitives and how they relate to one another. It’s the first post in a series, and upcoming posts cover our agentic operating system, background learning, proactive feeds, and much more. Triggers are the activation mechanism for getting work done, but they also carry instructions: a human message is both the moment of activation and the description of what to do. They are both the When? and the What? of a task. The type of trigger conditions the execution: a scheduled background task might stay conservative (for example, do nothing if uncertain), while a human-initiated one would be responsive (for example, ask rather than stop). We define an agent as a persistent, learning actor . It’s the Who? in any execution, and the anchor against which learning accrues. Two agents given identical input can differ, because they carry different instructions, capabilities, and histories. The agent isn’t the instructions it follows. It’s the entity that interprets them. It consists of three things: Everything else is extrinsic: the large language model (LLM) underlying the agent is a swappable model parameter, conversation history is per-session state, and triggers belong to the platform. A consequence of this definition is that a user request “ I want an agent that monitors my Slack and sends a digest every morning ” is usually a trigger added to an existing agent , not a new agent or workflow. With this framing, we can merge chat, scheduled, and “autonomous” agents into one actor that you can converse with, schedule, and that can orchestrate and inspect its own past work. Capabilities are How an agent acts, spanning a spectrum from fully agentic to fully deterministic. That axis is really a confidence contract : how much latitude the agent keeps versus how much the user fixes in advance. Tools are atomic operations with a typed schema: send an email, query a database, read a file. Whether a local function, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, or another agent behind a protocol boundary, the caller sees the same interface: name, description, parameters, result. Skills are structured guidance with room for judgment: instructions bundled with resources (templates, scripts, examples) that describe an approach rather than a rigid sequence. They load through progressive disclosure , so the agent sees only names and short descriptions until one becomes relevant, then reads the full instructions in. A skill can therefore bundle arbitrary depth of expertise without a constant cost. Workflows are deterministic coordination: declared steps, control flow, branching, and error handling that execute in fixed order, with decision logic in code rather than model inference. Think of a purchase-approval route: budget check, manager sign-off, then finance, each recorded. The route is fixed, but the judgment inside a step is still the agent’s. Figure 2: Skills versus workflows, which differ in whether the agent or the code decides the step order A natural question arises: if models keep improving, won’t skills and workflows become unnecessary? We don’t think so, because each holds value independent of model capability. Skills are the unit for capturing, versioning, and sharing institutional expertise, while workflows deliver auditability, step-wise visibility, and deterministic multi-service coordination. Nor are they fixed: a well-understood skill can tighten into a workflow ( crystallization ), a workflow that keeps hitting edge cases can loosen back into a skill ( dissolution ). This is done in Quick through our continuous learning framework, which we will describe in a future post. Return to “ monitor my Slack channel and send me a daily digest ”. Because these primitives compose, the same request can be met several valid ways: All three produce a daily digest on a schedule. What differs is the confidence contract. A user who trusts the agent wants the first, one burned by inconsistency the second, one running a compliance-sensitive process the third. Learning shifts that trajectory over time. A task that starts as one sentence (“ check my email for urgent items ”) accumulates domain-bound learnings: effective queries, preferred formatting, and which senders matter. The tenth run is markedly better, with no one encoding that by hand. The right design is the simplest option that meets the user’s confidence requirement, with a path to graduate through autonomous learning when they need more. The value of this agentic primitive taxonomy is that four plain questions, When , What , Who , and How , are enough to place any piece of agentic work, from a one-line chat request to a scheduled, compliance-grade process. Sharing one vocabulary lets builders reason about the system and lets the product hide complexity. Best of all, the user never has to learn any of it. They say what they want, and the system assembles the appropriate primitives to do their job. Next in the series: the agentic operating system that builds on these primitives and powers Amazon Quick.

“工程智慧” 為核心議題，共話智慧時代的前沿趨勢。 會上， 加拿大工程院外籍院士、智象元一（HiDream.ai）創始人兼 CEO 梅濤 發表演講，提出 構建智慧體化的全模態世界模型（Agentic Omnimodal World Models） ，邁向下一代世界智慧。 AI模型聚合平臺 進入自我加速軌道，模型迭代已按周推進。 AI 的能力越強，其短板也越不容忽視。在 數字智慧（Digital AI）領域 ，從文本互動、程式碼編寫到影片生成，乃至數學研究，AI 已達到甚至超越人類專家水平。以數學研究為例，最近OpenAI 一次性公開 377 項數學成果，覆蓋數百個長期懸而未決的開放問題。 物理智慧（Physical AI） 理解世界如何執行，並推演未來可能發生的事件。它通過對全模態資訊的統一理解與生成，對世界狀態、物理規律和因果關係進行建模，從而實現對真實世界的感知、推演與預測。 不同的技術路徑通往世界模型，這成為了AI發展的下一個競爭焦點。 當下產業界已經形成大語言、多模態和具身大模型三條演進路線。梅濤認為，三條技術路線並非彼此孤立，長遠來看終將匯流，走向 智慧體化世界模型（Agentic Omnimodal World Models） 。 智慧體化世界模型主要有三個部分: 第一， LLM ， 它是智慧體的決策大腦，負責理解意圖、生成推理、制定任務規劃。 第二，Omni-Model， 也就是通用世界模型。它是世界模擬器：基於LLM的意圖，模擬物理世界的執行，推演行動帶來的後果，並預判下一步動作。 第三，Embodied Context， 具身上下文。它對接真實的物理環境，負責執行具身行動，同時將真實觀測資料回傳，用於校準世界模型。 三者協同，實現 「One Token Space, One World」 ——在同一個Token空間裡，思維世界與物理世界實現統一。而這，正是通往下一代世界智慧的關鍵所在。 對世界模型的思考，內化而成了智象的產品哲學與技術基因。智象自研了 原生全模態（Unified Transformer）模型架構
